messages.body_plain:
Dear listfolk,

I am building a DSM for coastal cetaceans occurring in a small embayment (400-500 sq. km) and I have several questions, some technical, some a bit more philosophical. Apologies for the number of queries; I thought it best to combine them rather than write individual posts.

I have been working off the very thorough vignettes on pantropical dolphins and common loons found at https://github.com/dill/dsm/wiki/Examples. I am using R 3.1.1 and the latest version of packages dsm and Distance.

Q1. As with many biological datasets of elusive, intermittenly available species, many of my segments are associated with zero counts. What is the best way to deal with zero-inflation in a DSM context?

I have tried using a negative binomial and a Tweedie distribution. Both are obvious improvements over Poisson (from inspecting the residuals) yet my best model thus far only explains about 6% of the deviance (see residual plot attached) and most candidate models tested returned smaller (or sometimes negative!) %Dev. I am therefore wondering whether negbin and Tweedie are appropriate at all and whether I should explore alternative distributions such as those found in the gamlss package (e.g. zero-adjusted/inflated Poisson)?

Q2. What is the rationale behind the choice of maximum basis sizes in gams? In the common loon example, these are set to 10 for univariate smooths and 18 for bivariate smooths. Is this simply a judgement call?

Q3. Is multicollinearity (concurvity?) something to worry about in a DSM? It appears that neither the dolphin nor the loon examples investigate covariate relationships (e.g. via variance inflation factors) prior to model fitting. Is this because the particular gam formulation used is not sensitive to collinearity, or any other reason I may have missed?

Q4. I am trying to gain a sense for whether a soap film smoother would be justified in my case - my study area is in my view fairly complex (it includes mangrove areas, small river mouths etc.) and we know that cetaceans do not occur onshore so a soap film that reduces edge effects would appear sensible. In the common loon example however, no soap films were used despite the study area encompassing Rhode Island. Is there a reason why a soap film was not considered in that study? I would have thought regular smoothers would be prone to smoothing over the island.

Also, when a soap film is being used, are there any general guidelines on how to choose the number of knots in the make.soapgrid command? The soaps I have tried generally tend to produce much larger abundance estimates, mostly due to a single isolated "hotspot" of predicted abundance in a corner of the studya area away from where the majority of sightings have been made.

Q5. I calculated the size of my prediction grid cells in GIS but I would like to make sure I haven't missed anything obvious. The reason I ask is that in this recent post <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/distance-sampling/7-FZJDbW-fE>, Dave and Eric explained that cell sizes (444 sq km) could be obtained in GIS or from the width/height attributes of the cells in R.

However, in the Mexico dolphins example the grid cell centroids are situated approx.16 km apart (according to my GIS). This would correspond to a grid cell area of 16x16=256 sq km, not 444 sq km. This also contrasts with the height and width of preddata in R (32.072 and 37.065 km respectively) which give an area of 32.072 x 37.065 = 1189 sq km, again not 444 sq km ... so I am slightly confused. How was the value of 444 sqkm obtained?

Q6. Finally in Winiarski et al. (2013), <http://www.int-res.com/abstracts/meps/v492/p273-283/> the paper which accompanies the common loon example, the best detection function model (under AIC) was a hazard rate without covariates. The associated DSM thus used N as the response variable, but the equation on page 277 shows Nhat. Shouldn't this equation have shown N with an offset reflecting the effective area of the segment (calculated based on the estimated effective strip width) instead? What should one report in a paper when using density/abundance as the response?

Many thanks in advance for any thoughts/wisdom/advice anyone is willing to share.
Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil, hi listfolk,

I'm sure that most of them are certainly pertinent to folks on this list
engaged in building DSMs... I'll try to answer as much as I can, but
others should certainly chime in with their experiences

Q1. Zero-inflation: Worth considering here whether the model is truly
zero-inflated vs. just having many zeros. True zero-inflation would mean
too many zeros conditional on the model (as opposed to many in the
data). There are a few techniques to test this (though I don't have
personal experience of them): Broek (1995) and Yang, Hardin and Addy
(2010) (courtesy of Ben Bolker on StackOverflow).

I assume you're using nb() for the negative binomial response, so the
parameter is estimated at the same time as the other parameters (this is
much much faster than the old negbin() response). If that's not working
AND you have true zero-inflation AND you have count (as opposed to
estimated count/abundance) you could use the new ziplss() response which
implements a zero-inflated Poisson model (you may need to update mgcv
using update.packages() in R).

For what it's worth, I think your residual plots look okay. You may want
to use the dsm::rqgam.check() function to see if there is any real
structure in the resids vs fitted plot (see this slide
http://converged.yt/talks/duke-dsm/talk.html#%2850%29 and Dunn and Smyth
(1996) for more about randomised quantile residuals).

Q2. Basis size: This is a topic of some controversy as many folks think
that the size should be limited to allow for "realistic" covariate
effects (e.g. that if the resulting smooths are too wiggly this is not
very realistic). I have been more an advocate of letting the data tell
you what it can and although the resulting smooths may be wiggly on a
small scale, the broad trends are what we're interested in. There is
advice on choosing basis size in line with the latter philosophy in the
mgcv help page ?choose.k.

Q3. Concurvity: I haven't spent enough time really grappling with this
issue directly yet. What I have experienced is that there are
differences in which smooths are selected in the model, depending on
which of a series of covariates are removed first (or which are included
in the first place). This problem is less pronounced when using
method="REML" in my experience. (This is mainly folk story territory for
me at the moment.)

I did find the other day that mgcv has a function called concurvity()
that will estimate the concurvity between your smooths, this probably
bears more investigation.

Q4. Soap: We didn't use the soap film for the Rhode Island analysis
mainly due to a time constraint on our part. But I also note that there
wasn't evidence of leakage through the island in the resulting models
(e.g. see plots in
https://github.com/dill/MEPS-analysis/blob/master/MEPS-analysis.pdf).

Soap films can be tricky and frustrating to setup and fit, you may find
a script I wrote to check your knot setup useful:
https://github.com/dill/soap_checker I don't know about general
guidelines. I've had success in evenly spaced knots across the study
area, but the number of knots depends on the complexity of the spatial
component of the model. You may also need to increase the basis size of
the cyclic boundary smooth, via the k= argument.

Q5. Mexico data: This is a really good question and I'm embarrassed that
I'd not noticed this before. As far as I know the areas were calculated
by GIS before the data (originally form NOAA) was imported into a
Distance (for Windows) project. I then extracted the data from that
project and I had assumed that the data coming in from Distance were
correct. I will check this out and report back to the list. Thanks for
noticing this!!

Q6. Response: Both Nhat and N (i.e. estimated abundance per segment and
count per segment) can be used when no covariates are included in the
detection function (as can N be used when covariates are used, provided
that the covariates only vary at the scale of the segment).

BUT in this case for the final model it looks like we did use N (see the
MEPS-analysis.pdf linked above) though for the majority of the models we
used Nhat. I can't remember why we did this (maybe to de-complicate the
stats part of the paper, maybe space constraint), but I agree this is
misleading.

In general I would not do what we did and instead report exactly the
model used.

Hope this begins to clear up some of those questions, do ask for
elaboration on any of the above if that's useful.

All the best,
--dave

---

References

Broek, Jan van den. 1995. A Score Test for Zero Inflation in a Poisson
Distribution. Biometrics 51 (2): 738–43. doi:10.2307/2532959.

Dunn, PK, and GK Smyth. Randomized Quantile Residuals. Journal of
Computational and Graphical Statistics 5, no. 3 (1996): 236–244.

Yang, Zhao, James W. Hardin, and Cheryl L. Addy. 2010. “Score Tests for
Zero-Inflation in Overdispersed Count Data.” Communications in
Statistics - Theory and Methods 39 (11): 2008–30.
doi:10.1080/03610920902948228./03610920902948228#.VDVM81QUBAs

messages.body_plain:
On 27-30 October 2015 Duke Environmental Leadership program in
collaboration with the University of St Andrews will offer a workshop on
spatial modelling methods for distance sampling line transect data.

The workshop will cover: the basics of organizing survey data in ArcGIS
using the MGET toolbox, developed at the Marine Geospatial Ecology Lab,
Duke; followed by building and evaluating spatially explicit models of
abundance (using environmental predictors) in R, using packages
developed at the Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental
Modelling, St Andrews. The aim will be to demonstrate an end-to-end
workflow for spatial modelling of distance sampling data, and illustrate
the underlying theory behind both spatial modelling using generalized
additive models and distance sampling (we will focus on the "density
surface modelling" approach).

The course is intended for graduate students/postdocs/faculty in applied
ecology, government/industry scientists and wildlife managers interested
in developing spatially explicit models of abundance. Prior knowledge of
R and ArcGIS will be highly advantageous, as is a quantitative background.

The course will be taught by David L Miller (St Andrews), Jason J
Roberts (Duke) and Eric Rexstad (St Andrews), at the Duke campus in
Durham, NC.

The deadline for registration is 12 October 2015.

Detailed information on the course content and registration can be found
at https://nicholas.duke.edu/del/distance.

--

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am using the DSM package for the first time and using Dave Miller's vignette as a guide.  My question is whether the off.set parameter for predictions should be the effective area searched (or the effective half area) or whether it should be the size of the cell that I want predictions for (as implied by the vignette).  I want my predictions to be in terms of density (animals per km^2) at each of my prediction points, so I used offset = 1000*1000.  Is this correct?

Non-reproducible example code:

# Estimating the detection function with BF as a covariate
ds.model <- ds(flatfile, adjustment="cos", order=2, formula=~as.factor(BFDummy))

# Fitting a DSM model with a spline on latitude and longitude and yearday as a covariate
dsm.model <- dsm(Nhat~s(X,Y, k=30) + factor(YDay),
                 ds.model$ddf, seg.data, obs.data, family=Tweedie(p=1.20),
                 method="REML")

# Density predictions at each of the prediction points
predictions$DSM <- predict(dsm.model, predictions, off.set=1000*1000)

Thanks for your help!

Eiren

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Off.set term for DSM predictions
messages.body_plain:
Eiren:

The offset is used in conjunction with the function predict().  As a consequence, the value you specify for the offset is the size of your **prediction grid**.  You will have values everywhere throughout your study area for the predictors from which you constructed your density surface model.  In the example you provided, your predictors are X, Y and yearday.  Yearday will be the same throughout your prediction grid, but X and Y take on values dependent upon location within the prediction grid.  The size of the prediction grid cells are what you specify for the offset.

Hope that is helpful.

messages.body_plain:
Dear listfolk,

I am struggling with a zero-inflated density surface model (DSM) built using the new ziplss() response.

This is following some of David Miller's suggestions from earlier this month (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/distance-sampling/Z2Cbc3-VYG4).

The model is of the form:

zipdsm(list(N~s(x,y, m=c(1,.5)),~s(depth, m=1)+s(shore, m=1)),
             det.hn.cos2$ddf,
             seg.data,
             obs.data[obs.data$distance<=250,],
             family=ziplss())

Where the probability of presence is modelled as a function of both depth and distance from shore (in line with existing biological knowledge about the species) and the Poisson component is modelled as a bivariate smooth of x and y (transformed lat/lon).
zipdsm is a modified version of the dsm function tweaked to accomodate a formula in two parts as shown above.
The model runs smoothly and gives me a sensible abundance estimate.

However, I am facing two problems:

(1) ziplss returns warning messages to inform me that offsets are ignored.

1: In estimate.gam(G, method, optimizer, control, in.out, scale, gamma,  :
  sorry, general families currently ignore offsets

Given the importance of including segment areas as offsets, I am worried about this - but unsure how to work around it?

(2) I tried adapting the dsm.var.prop/dsm.var.gam to suit my zero-inflated model but without success.

I think I may be failing to properly retrieve/code the inverse link function, as it is a two-stage model.
There may also be issues with offsets if ziplss disregards them when they're needed.

Does anyone know how to solve this?

I have tried a quasipoisson model but it is greatly overdispersed and the residuals look terrible.
I also tried a negative binomial but I don't trust it. Although the residuals plots look better, the abundance estimates are through the roof and the predictive surface, when mapped, does not match sightings well. In addition, Zuur et al. (Zero Inflated models and generalized linear mixed models in R, p78) suggest that negative binomial models may return biased estimates in the presence of zero-inflation. This would explain the "weird" predictions I get with this model.

It is therefore critical that I try and make the ZI work.
Any inputs, thoughts, or advice will be immensely appreciated.

Thanks in advance,
Phil

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] sampling effort / multiplier
messages.body_plain:
Laura:

The easiest way to remember how to provide information to Distance about your survey is that you are describing the amount of effort associated with your survey.  One of the fundamental pieces of information needed for density estimation is the "encounter rate", which for line transects is the number of objects detected per metre (or kilometre) of effort.

Therefore, in your situation, effort is the length of the transect multiplied by the number of times the transect is walked.  That is the value you should provide to Distance when asked to provide line length for each transect.  You could do this as a multiplier, but only if all transects are visited the same number of times (because multipliers can only be applied for the entire study area).  Because your number of visits is not constant, your best solution is to enter line length times number of visits in the "effort" column.

As an aside, note that having 6 transects will make it difficult for you to obtain a good estimate of the variability in encounter rate between transects.  In the future, your study would be improved by increasing the number of transects in your study; both to improve the estimate of variability in encounter rate and to broaden the representativeness of your transects to the study area.

I will answer your second question (about clusters) separately so that the email thread is maintained.

Laura:

You are correct that detectability of animals may be enhanced when clusters are large.  That can be incorporated into analyses by treating cluster size as a covariate influencing the detection function.  However, it is fine to "ungroup" sightings as you say, and treat detections as multiple detections at the same perpendicular distance.  The consequence of this "ungrouping" was investigated via simulation by Buckland et al. (2010) in a paper entitled
Design and Analysis of Line Transect Surveys for Primates
published in International Journal of Primatology .
http://doi:10.1007/s10764-010-9431-5

Those consequences were found to be small (bias<0.13) when simulating groups of size 3-30.

> Laura:
>
> The easiest way to remember how to provide information to Distance about your survey is that you are describing the amount of effort associated with your survey.  One of the fundamental pieces of information needed for density estimation is the "encounter rate", which for line transects is the number of objects detected per metre (or kilometre) of effort.
>
> Therefore, in your situation, effort is the length of the transect multiplied by the number of times the transect is walked.  That is the value you should provide to Distance when asked to provide line length for each transect.  You could do this as a multiplier, but only if all transects are visited the same number of times (because multipliers can only be applied for the entire study area).  Because your number of visits is not constant, your best solution is to enter line length times number of visits in the "effort" column.
>
> As an aside, note that having 6 transects will make it difficult for you to obtain a good estimate of the variability in encounter rate between transects.  In the future, your study would be improved by increasing the number of transects in your study; both to improve the estimate of variability in encounter rate and to broaden the representativeness of your transects to the study area.
